title: Animate Your Character
tagline: Stop sliding a frozen drawing around. Make it move.
whenToUse: Any time after Lesson 2 (you need a character to animate). It shines most **during Lesson 9**, when students want their character to feel alive. Pairs naturally with Bonus Lesson A — image frames animate the same way. One period.
builtOn: Lesson 2 — your `MyCharacter` drawing. You will reuse it directly.
goals: Understand animation as a flipbook: several still pictures shown fast, one after another
Draw your character in two to four slightly different **poses**
Use `AnimatedSprite` to hold those poses and flip between them automatically

vocab.def: one still picture in the flipbook — one **pose** of your character
one version of your character's drawing. Mouth open vs. closed, legs together vs. apart
a library object that holds several frame sprites and draws one at a time
how many **game** frames each picture stays on screen. `8` means "hold each pose for 8 game frames." Smaller is faster

warmup: Have you ever made a flipbook in the corner of a notebook? How does a cartoon make a character walk? It is just drawings, shown fast. And remember from Lesson 1 — `draw()` is already a flipbook, drawing a new picture about 60 times a second.

howItWorks.h: Two different things are both called a frame
p: This is worth getting straight before anything else, because the word does double duty.
A **game frame** is one run of `draw()` — about 60 of them every second. You have known this since Lesson 1.
An **animation frame** is one picture in your flipbook — one pose of your character.
`setFrameRate(8)` is what connects them: hold each animation frame for 8 game frames.

howItWorks.h: A frame is just a drawing you already know how to make
p: A frame class is your Lesson 2 character with one addition: a `pose` number. The same class draws several slightly different versions depending on that number.

code.label: One class, several poses

bullets: **Only change what should move.** Keep everything else identical between poses, or it looks like flickering instead of animation.

p: This is the one genuinely new line in the lesson. You chain the calls together to build up the flipbook.

code.label: Three poses into one animated sprite
code.body:
player = AnimatedSprite.FromSprite(new MyCharacterFrame(this, width/2, height/2, 0))
    .AddFrameSprite(new MyCharacterFrame(this, width/2, height/2, 1))
    .AddFrameSprite(new MyCharacterFrame(this, width/2, height/2, 2))
    .setFrameRate(8);

bullets: `FromSprite(...)` starts the flipbook with the first page.
`AddFrameSprite(...)` adds another page. Add as many as you like.
`setFrameRate(8)` sets how long each page stays up.
**Create every frame at the SAME x and y.** If you do not, your character visibly jumps every time the page turns.

howItWorks.h: Frame rate is backwards from what you would guess
p: `setFrameRate()` is **game frames per picture** — how long to hold each pose. So a **smaller** number means a **faster** animation.
`setFrameRate(4)` is fast and frantic. `setFrameRate(20)` is slow and calm. The smallest allowed is 1, and the default is 8 if you never call it.

howItWorks.h: Everything else works exactly as before
p: An `AnimatedSprite` is still a sprite. `move()`, `followMouse()`, `keyboardControl()` — all the same as Lessons 3 and 4.
`drawSprite()` draws the current pose **and** turns the page for you. You do not have to manage any of it.

howItWorks.h: One honest catch, if you are using this in Lesson 9
p: An `AnimatedSprite` is **not** a `Blob`, so `collidesWith()` is not available on it. That is the trade for getting animation.
Use `distanceTo()` instead. It works between any two sprites:

code.label: Collision without collidesWith

bullets: Pick a number that matches your character's size. Bigger is more forgiving, exactly like the radius was.

steps: Copy your **whole character drawing** from your Lesson 2 `MyCharacter` tab into it, then rename the class and constructor to `MyCharacterFrame`.
Add the `int pose;` field and the `this.pose = pose;` line in the constructor, matching the starter code below.
Pick **one** thing on your character to animate — the mouth is easiest. Legs, arms, wings, or ears also work well.
Wrap just that part in an `if (pose == 0) { ... } else if (pose == 1) { ... }`. Make the difference small.
In your main sketch, build the `AnimatedSprite` from two frames. **Both at the same x and y.**
Run it. Your character should be flipping between two poses on its own.
Add a third pose. Then try `setFrameRate(4)` and `setFrameRate(20)` and see which speed suits your character.
Move it: add `player.followMouse()` or arrow-key control, exactly like Lesson 4. Animation and motion work together with no extra effort.
If your character jumps or twitches when the pose changes, two things to check: are all frames at the same x and y, and are the non-moving parts truly identical between poses?

Main sketch tab

makeItYours: Add a fourth pose. Try animating **legs or arms** instead of the mouth — make it walk.
Change `setFrameRate()`. Try `4` (fast and frantic) and `20` (slow and calm). Which one is your character?
Add more frames for smoother motion. More pages means a smoother flipbook.
Make a second animated creature — a pet? — with its own `setVelocity()` drifting across the scene.
**Plug it into your Lesson 9 game.** Remember: use `distanceTo()` instead of `collidesWith()`, because an `AnimatedSprite` is not a `Blob`.
challenge: Take manual control of the flipbook. Instead of letting it auto-advance, call `nextFrame()` or `setFrameNumber(n)` on a key press to trigger a specific pose — a jump, an attack, a blink. That is how real games do special moves.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "my character jumps around when it animates", "my animation is too fast", or "how do I use an AnimatedSprite in my Lesson 9 game with collisions?" Paste in your frame class if the poses look wrong.
wrapup: What is the difference between a game frame and an animation frame? What does `setFrameRate(4)` do compared to `setFrameRate(20)`?
assignmentTask: Bring your character to life with at least two poses flipping automatically.
assignmentDo: Make a `MyCharacterFrame` class with a `pose` number, based on your Lesson 2 character.
Draw at least two poses that differ in **one** thing. Keep everything else identical.
Build an `AnimatedSprite` with `FromSprite(...).AddFrameSprite(...)`, creating every frame at the same x and y.
Set a frame rate that suits the motion you are going for.
Move it in `draw()` — `followMouse()` or arrow keys, your choice.
submit: A short screen recording — a screenshot cannot show an animation, so this one really needs to be a recording.

checklist: Draw my character in two or more slightly different poses (frames).
Move and draw my animated character in `draw()`.
standard: Build a multi-frame animated character with `AnimatedSprite` and control its animation speed.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: My character appears and flips between poses on its own.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and the animation is my own — my poses, my character, and a frame rate that looks right for the motion I want.

stages.text: …and I took it further — wired the animation into my Lesson 9 game with `distanceTo()`, animated a second creature, hand-controlled a pose on a key press, or animated image frames.

thinking: In one or two sentences: what part of your character did you make move, and what frame rate looked right for it?

di.h: The flipbook idea — connect it to Lesson 1
p: Animation is a few still pictures, shown quickly in order, looping. Every student already understands this from notebook flipbooks.

Make the connection explicit: **`draw()` is the flipbook engine** they have had since Lesson 1. `AnimatedSprite` is the flipbook the engine flips through. Nothing new is happening underneath — they are just adding pages.

di.h: Name the two meanings of "frame" up front
p: A **game frame** is one run of `draw()` (~60/sec, from Lesson 3). An **animation frame** is one picture in the flipbook.
Say both out loud before showing `setFrameRate()`, or the number will make no sense to anyone.

di.h: The frame class — it is their Lesson 2 character
p: A frame is just a drawing, exactly like `MyCharacter`. The only addition is a `pose` number so the same class can draw a few variations.
Demonstrate: keep the body and eyes identical, change **only** the mouth between poses.
"Only change what should move — keep everything else identical, or it looks jittery." This is the single most important piece of art advice in the lesson.
`AnimatedSprite.FromSprite(first).AddFrameSprite(next).AddFrameSprite(next).setFrameRate(8)`
"`FromSprite` starts the flipbook, `AddFrameSprite` adds another page, `setFrameRate` sets the speed." Do not explain method chaining as a concept — just read it left to right.
**CRUCIAL: create every frame at the SAME x, y**, or the character visibly jumps when the page turns. Say this while you type it.

di.h: setFrameRate is a ratio, and it is backwards
p: It is game-frames-**per-picture**, not pictures-per-second. **Smaller is faster.** Minimum is 1. Default is 8 if never called.
Demo `setFrameRate(4)` and then `setFrameRate(20)` back to back on the projector. The direction only lands once they see it.

di.h: The Lesson 9 caveat — say it clearly
p: `AnimatedSprite` extends `CompoundSprite`, **not** `Blob`, so it has **no `collidesWith()`**. This is the one thing that will trip up a student who brings animation into their capstone.
The fix is `distanceTo(otherSprite) < threshold`. `distanceTo()` is inherited from `Sprite` and works between any two sprites.
Do not hide this. A student who discovers it mid-capstone with no warning loses a whole period.

guided: New tab `MyCharacterFrame`. Students paste in their **own** Lesson 2 character drawing, then rename the class and constructor.
Add the `int pose` field and `this.pose = pose;` together.
Make pose 0 and pose 1 differ in exactly **one** thing — the mouth. Do this as a class so everyone sees how small the difference should be.
In the main tab, build the `AnimatedSprite` from two frames and run it. Watch it talk. This is the payoff moment.
As a class, try `setFrameRate(4)`, then `setFrameRate(20)`. Ask which suits their character.
Release to personalize: more poses, animating legs or arms, a second creature.
If students are mid-capstone, spend the last ten minutes on the `distanceTo()` swap so they can actually use this in their game.
pitfalls: **Frames created at different x, y.** The character teleports on every page turn. The most common and most confusing bug in this lesson.
**Poses that differ too much.** It reads as flickering, not animation. Push them to change one thing.
**Expecting a bigger `setFrameRate()` to mean faster.** It is the opposite.
**Calling `collidesWith()` on an `AnimatedSprite`.** It will not compile. Use `distanceTo()`.
Forgetting `this.pose = pose;` in the constructor, so every frame draws pose 0 and nothing appears to animate.
Forgetting to rename the constructor when copying from `MyCharacter` — a constructor whose name does not match its class becomes a method that never runs.
Not calling `drawSprite()` in `draw()`, so the flipbook never advances.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: A game frame is one run of `draw()` (~60/sec). An animation frame is one picture in the flipbook. `setFrameRate(4)` holds each picture for 4 game frames (fast); `setFrameRate(20)` holds it for 20 (slow).
notes: Only the current frame is drawn, so the Blob's plain circle never appears — `drawSprite()` is overridden in `MyCharacterFrame`. The radius and color in `super()` are just carried along.
**This lesson lands best during Lesson 9**, when students are already looking at their character and wishing it felt alive.

Ties into Bonus A: a frame can be an `ImageSprite`, so a sprite sheet animates with exactly the same pattern — `AnimatedSprite.FromSprite(new ImageSprite(this, x, y, "walk0.png")).AddFrameSprite(...)`.

Show the **AnimatedSceneExample** (File → Examples → Contributed Libraries → SpriteGame). Its clouds and sun are built with exactly this `FromSprite`/`AddFrameSprite` pattern, and seeing it in a finished scene is motivating.
Fast finishers: control the frame by hand instead of auto-advancing — `nextFrame()` or `setFrameNumber(n)` on a key press for a jump or attack pose.
Two poses is genuinely enough for a good result. Do not let students get stuck trying to draw eight.
